parts.name: Spire
parts.desc: A smooth toothless collar with the strike ring flared out at the crown, so it lands higher than anything else in the box and starts coming apart the moment somebody lands one back.
parts.rationale: Sibling 1-90, the tall attack stock. strikeHigh 1.64 sits 25.5 percent above the Tier 1 ceiling of 1.40; it buys that with a crown ring flared above the body, so it strikes at ratio 1.09 of height over 60 where the stock 1-90 sits at 0.93. Paid with lock 0.26, 39.7 percent below the Tier 1 floor of 0.55, which is further than the push: there are no teeth at all, only thread friction, so burstResist lands near a quarter of a normal build and one connected blow starts the wear cascade. Mass stays at 0.0058, equal to 1-90, because a 90mm body has to be thin walled or the top is unliftable off the launcher; that keeps mass out of the trade entirely.

parts.name: Belfry
parts.desc: Eleven teeth on a tall skeleton body, so it hits high and nothing will burst it, but there is almost no metal left in it to soak up a hit.
parts.rationale: Sibling 4-80, the tall attack ratchet. lock 1.46 is 24.7 percent above the Tier 1 ceiling of 1.28 and stays on the tooth ladder, eleven teeth at roughly 0.55 plus 0.081 per tooth. Paid with mass 0.0050, 33.3 percent under the Tier 1 floor of 0.0058, because the body between the teeth is drilled to a lattice; shock drain divides by mass and radius, so a light top loses more spin per hit and gets shoved further toward the rail, which is a real cost on the brawler chassis this part is for. strikeHigh 1.20 stays inside the range at ratio 0.90 of height over 60, dead in the stock drift band, so the part is not also a reach upgrade over 4-80.

parts.name: Deadbolt
parts.desc: Eleven teeth in a short heavy collar that simply will not come apart, fitted with a strike face buried so far under the blade that it can barely bother anybody.
parts.rationale: Sibling 9-60, the Tier 1 lock leader, with 8-30 as the geometry cousin. lock 1.46 is 24.7 percent past the ceiling on the same eleven tooth ring. Paid with strikeHigh 0.16, 31.9 percent below the Tier 1 floor of 0.46 and further than the push; the whole collar is tooth ring and the strike band is shrouded under the blade skirt, which is the only honest way a part ends up at ratio 0.32 of its own height. That guts both of its offensive uses at once, since the same number scales the tilt it puts on the other top and the burst wear it inflicts. Mass 0.0082 sits at the Tier 1 ceiling because eleven teeth in a 30mm body is the most metal the mount holds.

parts.name: Ballast
parts.desc: A solid slug of a collar that shrugs off shoves and sits low, held on a plain thread with no detents in it at all.
parts.rationale: Sibling 7-40, same height and same strike plane. mass 0.0088 is 25 percent above the Tier 1 ceiling of 0.0082, a solid slug with no through holes; shock drain divides by mass so it eats hits well, and the load term turns positive on any weighted build, so the spin bill is real. Paid with lock 0.29, 35.6 percent under the floor and further than the push, on a smooth thread with no teeth; burstResist falls to roughly a third of stock, so the answer to it is one clean connected blow. strikeHigh 0.58 is copied from 7-40 at ratio 0.87, inside the stock drift band.

parts.name: Millstone
parts.desc: The heaviest short collar in the workshop, lovely to grind behind and completely unable to reach over anybody.
parts.rationale: Sibling 8-30. mass 0.0088 is 25 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and it sits at the lowest legal height, so the centre of gravity term of 0.5 lifts absorb by about 23 percent and stable by about 19 percent and slows precession; that is the grinder package. Paid with strikeHigh 0.14, 34 percent below the floor and further than the push, from a strike band recessed inside the skirt at ratio 0.28 of height; it cannot topple or burst anybody and has to win by still spinning. Six teeth give lock 1.04, matching 6-50 on the tooth ladder, so the lock is honest rather than free.

parts.name: Latchwork
parts.desc: A fine eleven tooth ring cut into a drilled out body, unburstable and so light that every hit moves it.
parts.rationale: Sibling 5-60. lock 1.46 is 24.7 percent past the ceiling on the eleven tooth ring. Paid with mass 0.0051, 29.2 percent under the floor and further than the push, because the body is drilled out between the teeth; it takes more spin from every hit and travels further when shoved, which is what stops a burst proof ratchet from being a free fit. strikeHigh 0.82 is the stock number for a 60mm body at ratio 0.82, matching 9-60. This is the neutral height member of the eleven tooth family; Belfry is the tall one and Deadbolt is the short heavy one, and the three differ in strike plane and mass rather than in lock.

parts.name: Foundry Sleeve
parts.desc: A thick cast sleeve at normal height that takes a shove like a wall and comes apart on one clean strike.
parts.rationale: Sibling 3-60, the balance stock. mass 0.0088 is 25 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling as a thick walled cast sleeve; paid with lock 0.30, 34.2 percent under the floor and further than the push, on a smooth thread. It shares its trade with Ballast on purpose and separates from it by geometry: Ballast puts the same metal at 40mm and hits low at 0.58, this one keeps the normal strike plane at 0.86 and pays for the extra 20mm in faster precession, less absorb and less stable. Ratio 0.86 of height over 60 is inside the stock drift band.

parts.name: Portcullis
parts.desc: Fourteen coarse teeth in a collar that never seats fully, so it rides very low and very steady while the play in the thread lets it pop.
parts.rationale: Sibling 9-60. lock 1.70 is 57.5 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling, fourteen teeth on the same ladder of 0.55 plus 0.081 per tooth. Loose Lock then halves burstResist to an effective 0.85, which is below stock 9-60, and lifts stable by 30 percent; at 30mm the cogH term stacks on that, so wStable drops from about 306 to about 265 and it is the hardest top in the game to knock over. That is the drawback's own description made literal, and it is what keeps the mean honest: the extreme number on the card is halved before the simulation ever reads it, so the ceiling is a defensive wall and the mean is dragged back by every burst it eats. Paid with strikeHigh 0.14, 34 percent under the floor from a shrouded strike band at ratio 0.28, so it can never convert its survival into a knockout or a burst of its own. Mass 0.0082 sits at the Tier 1 ceiling.

parts.name: Weathervane
parts.desc: A flared crown that strikes above its own height and rings every one of those blows straight back through its own teeth.
parts.rationale: Sibling 1-90. strikeHigh 1.80 is 42.6 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling at ratio 1.20 of height over 60, a crown ring flared above the body; nothing else in the slot destabilises a top or wears a lock like it, since that one number scales both the tilt bump and the burst wear it inflicts. Paid with mass 0.0048, 41.7 percent under the floor, on a spun tube body, so it loses more spin per hit taken and is easy to shove out. Two teeth give lock 0.71, matching stock 2-70, so the lock is not a gift. Shear is the real price: its own strikes come back through its teeth at full wear instead of the 14 percent every other part pays, and because wear scales with the cube of impulse, the blow big enough to burst them is the blow most likely to burst it. Enormous ceiling, mean held down by its own best hits.

parts.name: Ingot
parts.desc: A dead weight of a collar on a thread worn smooth, putting everything it has into the first strike it lands and almost nothing into the rest.
parts.rationale: Sibling 6-50, identical geometry and identical strike plane at 0.70, ratio 0.84. mass 0.0096 is 58.3 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling, a solid slug with no tooth ring and no lightening holes at all; it resists shock drain, and on any weighted build the load term charges it spin the whole round. Paid with lock 0.20, 47.9 percent under the floor, from a thread worn smooth with no detents, leaving it about a quarter of the burst resistance of its sibling. One Shot makes the first strike it lands do triple wear and everything after it 40 percent, so the whole part is a single burst attempt: land the opener and the round is over, miss it and you are running a chassis that pops to any real blow and can no longer threaten one back. Ceiling very high, mean pulled under by the failed attempts.

notes:
SLOT: ratchet. 7 Forged, 3 Relic. No ids collide with the ten in sim2.js; the only hyphens anywhere are inside part codes.

ONE NEW DRAWBACK, and only one. Shear, for Weathervane. It is a change to an existing quantity, the striker's own wear share, not a special case. Add to DRAWBACKS: { id: 'shear', name: 'Shear', desc: 'Every blow it lands rings back through its own teeth at full force.' } and change the one line at sim2.js:842 from agg.wear += wear * K.burstBack / agg.spec.burstResist; to: agg.wear += wear * ((agg.spec.dw && agg.spec.dw.shear) ? 1 : K.burstBack) / agg.spec.burstResist; Nothing else moves. The other two Relics use looselock and oneshot, which the build and collide code already read.

TIER 1 RANGES USED, all measured against the ten stock ratchets: mass 0.0058 to 0.0082, width 0.0024; lock 0.55 to 1.28, width 0.73; strikeHigh 0.46 to 1.40, width 0.94. A 25 percent push is therefore 0.0006 on mass, 0.1825 on lock and 0.235 on strikeHigh. Every Forged pushes one stat between 24.7 and 25.5 percent past the range and pays with another between 29.2 and 39.7 percent past the opposite bound, so the payment is always the larger move.

HEIGHT IS NOT A PUSHABLE STAT. The mount spec in HANDOFF section 11 fixes ratchet bodies to 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, so every part here sits on one of those seven values. Height is also never a benefit in this simulation: it only raises precession through cogH, cuts absorb by cogH^0.30 and cuts stable by cogH^0.25. That is why the parts that pay in strikeHigh live at 30 to 50 and the parts that push it live at 90; a tall body with a low strike plane would be strictly bad and I did not author one.

THE DRIFT RULE I HELD TO. Stock parts sit at strikeHigh between 0.82 and 0.933 of height over 60. Anything in this proposal whose strikeHigh is neither pushed nor paid stays inside that band: Belfry 0.90, Ballast 0.87, Latchwork 0.82, Foundry Sleeve 0.86, Ingot 0.84. A part only leaves the band in the direction it is spending: a pushed strike plane comes from a crown ring flared above the body, ratio 1.09 on Spire and 1.20 on Weathervane, and a paid strike plane comes from a strike band shrouded under the blade skirt, ratio 0.32 on Deadbolt and 0.28 on Millstone and Portcullis. This is also the guard that stops power creep, because it is what forbids a part that hits like an 80 while standing like a 50.

TEETH TRACK LOCK on the ladder the stock parts already describe, lock is close to 0.55 plus 0.0811 per tooth: 2 teeth 0.71, 6 teeth 1.04, 11 teeth 1.46, 14 teeth 1.70. Within a single tooth count, thread fit and detent depth set the spread, which is why the four toothless parts run 0.20 to 0.30 while stock 0-70 keeps a detent shoulder at 0.55. Across tooth counts the ordering stays monotonic.

MASS TRACKS THE METAL. Heavy parts are short and solid, 0.0088 to 0.0096 at 30 to 60mm. Light parts are either 90mm thin walled tubes or bodies drilled to a lattice between the teeth. Nothing here is both tall and heavy, and nothing is both light and solid.

ACCEPTANCE GATE. Every one of the three Relics carries its cost as burst exposure, which is the measurable the audit will move. Portcullis has its headline lock halved by its own drawback before build() finishes, so its effective burstResist of 0.85 is below stock 9-60 and its gain is stability, not survivability. Weathervane pays for the largest strike plane in the slot by wearing itself at full rate on exactly its biggest hits, where the cubic impulse term bites hardest. Ingot has roughly a quarter of stock burst resistance and one usable strike. If partaudit 800 2 shows any of them more than 4 mean points over its named sibling, the cheapest correction in each case is the paid stat and not the pushed one: Portcullis strikeHigh 0.14 to 0.10, Weathervane mass 0.0048 to 0.0046, Ingot lock 0.20 to 0.16. Do not trim the pushed number, that is the part.

NAMING. Stock ratchets use the code as the name. These carry a word so the player can tell a Forged part from a stock one on the rail; the code stays the id and the workshop can render them as Deadbolt 11-30 if you want both visible. No name collides with an existing part in any slot, and Anvil and Collar were avoided because a blade and an assist already use them.

I edited nothing. This is a proposal only.
